content: Citric acid is a weak organic acid naturally found in citrus fruits. It serves as a natural preservative and is commonly used to impart a sour taste to foods and beverages, including soft drinks. In biochemistry, citric acid plays a crucial role as an intermediate in the citric acid cycle (Krebs cycle), which is essential for the metabolism of nearly all living organisms. Additionally, it functions as an environmentally friendly cleaning agent and acts as an antioxidant. While citric acid is present in various fruits and vegetables, it is most concentrated in lemons and limes, where it can constitute up to 8% of the fruit's dry weight. At room temperature, citric acid appears as a white crystalline powder. It can exist in two forms: anhydrous (water-free) or as a monohydrate. The anhydrous form crystallizes from hot water, whereas the monohydrate form crystallizes from cold water. Heating the monohydrate above 74°C converts it into the anhydrous form. Citric acid is also soluble in absolute ethanol, with 76 parts of citric acid dissolving in 100 parts of ethanol at 15°C. Chemically, citric acid shares properties with other carboxylic acids. When heated above 175°C, it decomposes, releasing carbon dioxide and water. The discovery of citric acid is attributed to the 8th-century alchemist Jabir Ibn Hayyan (Geber). By the 13th century, European scholars were aware of the acidic nature of lemon and lime juices, as documented in the encyclopedia Speculum Majus by Vincent of Beauvais. In 1784, Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele first isolated citric acid by crystallizing it from lemon juice. Industrial production began in 1860, leveraging the Italian citrus fruit industry. In 1893, C. Wehmer discovered that the mold Penicillium could produce citric acid from sugar. However, microbial production became industrially significant during World War I, when Italian citrus exports were disrupted. In 1917, American food chemist James Currie identified strains of the mold Aspergillus niger as efficient producers of citric acid, leading to large-scale production by Pfizer in 1919. The modern industrial production of citric acid primarily involves feeding Aspergillus niger cultures with sucrose or glucose-containing media, such as corn steep liquor, molasses, or hydrolyzed corn starch. After the mold is filtered out, citric acid is precipitated as calcium citrate using lime (calcium hydroxide) and then regenerated by treatment with sulfuric acid. In the Krebs cycle, citric acid is one of the key compounds involved in the physiological oxidation of fats, proteins, and carbohydrates into carbon dioxide and water. This series of chemical reactions is central to nearly all metabolic processes and provides two-thirds of the energy derived from food in higher organisms. The cycle was discovered by Sir Hans Adolf Krebs, who received the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this work. The cycle is also known as the citric acid cycle, the Krebs cycle, or the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. As a food additive, citric acid is used as a flavoring agent and preservative in foods and beverages, particularly soft drinks, and is designated by the E number E330. Citrate salts of various metals are used in dietary supplements to deliver minerals in a biologically available form. The buffering properties of citrates are employed to control pH in household cleaners and pharmaceuticals. In the United States, the Food Chemical Codex (FCC), published by the United States Pharmacopeia (USP), defines the purity requirements for citric acid as a food additive. Citric acid's ability to chelate metals makes it useful in soaps and laundry detergents, as it allows these cleaners to function effectively in hard water by chelating metal ions. It is also used to regenerate ion exchange materials in water softeners by removing accumulated metal ions as citrate complexes. In biotechnology and the pharmaceutical industry, citric acid is used to passivate high-purity process piping as an alternative to nitric acid, which is hazardous to dispose of. Citric acid is also an active ingredient in some bathroom and kitchen cleaning solutions. A 6% citric acid solution can remove hard water stains from glass without scrubbing. In industrial applications, it is used to dissolve rust from steel. Citric acid is also employed as a buffer to increase the solubility of brown heroin. Single-use citric acid sachets are distributed in harm reduction programs to encourage heroin users to exchange dirty needles for clean ones, reducing the spread of diseases like AIDS and hepatitis. Other acidifiers, such as ascorbic acid, acetic acid, and lactic acid, are also used for this purpose, but in their absence, users may substitute lemon juice or vinegar. Citric acid is also a precursor in the synthesis of HMTD, a highly sensitive explosive, and large purchases of citric acid may raise suspicions of potential terrorist activity. In food preparation, citric acid can be added to ice cream to prevent fat globules from clumping and can substitute for fresh lemon juice in recipes. It is also used in bath salts, bath bombs, and grease-cleaning products. When applied to hair, citric acid opens the cuticle layer, allowing deeper penetration into the hair shaft. It is used in shampoos to remove wax and coloring from hair and is a component of the product Sun-In for bleaching, though it is generally not recommended due to the damage it can cause. Citric acid is also used as a stop bath in photography, where its mild acidity neutralizes the alkaline developer, enhancing the effectiveness of the stop bath compared to plain water. Citric acid is recognized as safe for use in food by all major national and international food regulatory agencies. It is naturally present in almost all forms of life, and excess citric acid is readily metabolized and eliminated from the body. However, dietary intolerance to citric acid has been reported, though it is rare and often described as a pseudo-allergic reaction. Contact with dry citric acid or concentrated solutions can cause skin and eye irritation, necessitating the use of protective clothing when handling these materials. Excessive consumption of citric acid can erode tooth enamel, and close contact with the eyes may cause a burning sensation or, in severe cases, loss of sight. There have been erroneous claims that E330 (citric acid) is a major cause of cancer. This misconception likely arises from confusion over the word Krebs, which refers to Sir Hans Adolf Krebs, the discoverer of the Krebs cycle, and not the German word for cancer. Citric acid is not known to be harmful to the body when consumed alone.
